batchName: Empire: Tiberius and Caligula (AD 14-41) - Medium Batch 2

questions.question: Caligula was murdered the day before he was due to leave for which city?
questions.explanation: On 24 January AD 41, the day before he was to set out for Alexandria, Caligula was stabbed in a passage beneath his palace during a festival of games.
questions.sourceQuote: On 24 January AD 41, the day before he was due to leave for Alexandria, Egypt's great city, the emperor Caligula was stabbed in a narrow passage beneath his palace during a festival of games.

questions.question: Where did Germanicus fall ill and die in AD 19, convinced he had been poisoned?
questions.explanation: Germanicus died at Antioch, Syria's chief city, after a bitter quarrel with the governor of Syria. Rumours that Tiberius was behind his death never faded.
questions.sourceQuote: In October AD 19 he fell ill at Antioch, Syria's chief city, and died convinced he had been poisoned.

questions.question: One modern scholar counted how many people accused of treason during Tiberius's 22-year reign?
questions.explanation: The count was no more than 52, and nearly half escaped conviction. That challenges the ancient picture of a reign of terror.
questions.sourceQuote: One counted no more than 52 people accused of treason in Tiberius's 22-year reign, nearly half of whom escaped conviction.

questions.question: How did Germanicus end the mutiny of the Rhine legions in AD 14?
options: He paid them out of his own pocket
He asked Tiberius to send the Guard
He let them proclaim him emperor
questions.explanation: Germanicus covered the troops' unpaid bonuses himself and then led them into Germany. He spent three years fighting the war leader behind the Teutoburg disaster.
questions.sourceQuote: He refused, paid them out of his own pocket, and led them into Germany.

questions.question: Tiberius discouraged worship of himself, allowing only one temple in his honour. Where was it?
questions.explanation: The single temple Tiberius allowed stood at Smyrna, a Greek city in western Turkey. This fits his general dislike of grand honours.
questions.sourceQuote: He also discouraged worship of himself, allowing just one temple in his honour, at Smyrna, a Greek city in western Turkey.

questions.question: A Jewish writer who visited Caligula's court called which period a "Golden Age"?
options: His childhood in the army camps
The final year before his murder
The first seven months of his reign
questions.explanation: The writer praised the first seven months of Caligula's rule. That opening was marked by cash gifts, lavish games and a doubled Guard bonus.
questions.sourceQuote: A Jewish writer who later visited his court called the first seven months a "Golden Age".

questions.question: Why did moving the Praetorian Guard into Rome itself make Sejanus so powerful?
options: It placed the imperial treasury in his barracks
It let him sit in the Senate as a consul
It gave him command of the Rhine legions
It put 6,000-9,000 soldiers under him inside the capital
It made him head of the city's grain supply
questions.explanation: Once Tiberius moved the Guard from camps outside Rome into the city, Sejanus had thousands of soldiers in the capital. Tiberius came to call him "partner of my labours".
questions.sourceQuote: When the emperor Tiberius moved the Guard from camps outside Rome into the city itself, Sejanus gained between 6,000 and 9,000 soldiers inside the capital.

questions.question: After Caligula's murder, what did some senators talk of doing?
options: Choosing a new emperor by public vote
questions.explanation: Some senators spoke of bringing back the Republic, but the Praetorians had other plans. They proclaimed Caligula's uncle emperor.
questions.sourceQuote: In the Senate, some spoke of restoring the Republic, government without emperors.

questions.question: How did senators interpret Tiberius's refusal of honours such as the Civic Crown?
options: As an insult to Augustus's memory
As a sign he planned to restore the Republic
As proof he was in poor health
questions.explanation: Senators saw his refusals as hypocrisy, and relations soured. His vague instructions to the Senate made things worse.
questions.sourceQuote: Senators read this as hypocrisy, not humility, and relations soured.

questions.question: Caligula's floating bridge of ships, over 3 km long, linked the resort of Baiae to which nearby port?
questions.explanation: The bridge ran from Baiae to Puteoli, and Caligula rode Incitatus across it. Its pointlessness may have been the point: a display of total power.
questions.sourceQuote: In AD 39 or 40 he built a floating bridge of ships more than 3 km (two miles) long, from Baiae, a seaside resort near Naples, to the nearby port of Puteoli.
